title: Tax Basics for Teens
description: Learn the fundamentals of Canadian taxes, understand your first paycheque, and discover why filing a tax return matters even for part-time workers.
learningObjectives: Understand what taxes are and how they fund government services
Read and interpret your first paycheque deductions
Learn why teens should file tax returns

content.introduction: Taxes are contributions that Canadians make to fund important services we all use - from schools and hospitals to roads and parks.

sections.heading: Why Do We Pay Taxes?
sections.content: Every time you use a public service - riding the bus to school, visiting a doctor, or checking out a library book - you're using something paid for by taxes. Taxes are how we pool our money together to pay for things that benefit everyone.

sections.heading: Types of Taxes in Canada
sections.content: There are several types of taxes you'll encounter:

types.name: Income Tax
types.description: Tax on money you earn from working. This is taken off your paycheque automatically.
types.example: If you earn $1,000, about $50-150 might go to income tax

types.name: Sales Tax (GST/HST)
types.description: Tax added when you buy things. Rate varies by province (5-15%).
types.example: A $10 item might cost $11.30 after tax in Ontario

types.name: Property Tax
types.description: Tax on owning property (your parents probably pay this).
types.example: Annual tax on houses, apartments, land

sections.heading: Federal vs Provincial Taxes
sections.content: In Canada, both the federal government and your provincial government collect income tax. That's why you see two deductions on your paycheque!

breakdown.federal: Goes to Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for national programs
breakdown.provincial: Stays in your province for local services

interactive.title: Where Does Your Tax Dollar Go?
interactive.instruction: Click each slice to see what your taxes pay for!

keyTakeaways: Taxes fund services we all use every day
You pay income tax on earnings and sales tax on purchases
Both federal and provincial governments collect income tax
Understanding taxes helps you make better financial decisions

content.introduction: Your first paycheque can be confusing! You worked 20 hours at $15/hour ($300 gross), but only got $255 deposited. Where did $45 go? Let's break it down.

sections.heading: Gross vs Net Income
sections.content: These are two important terms you'll see on every paycheque:

terms.definition: Total amount you earned BEFORE any deductions
Amount you actually receive AFTER deductions

sections.tip: Always negotiate salary based on GROSS income, but budget based on NET income!

sections.heading: Common Paycheque Deductions
sections.content: Here's what typically comes off your paycheque:

deductions.name: CPP (Canada Pension Plan)
deductions.note: You get this money back when you retire!

deductions.name: EI (Employment Insurance)
deductions.description: Insurance if you lose your job
deductions.note: Protects you if you're laid off

sections.heading: Reading Your Pay Stub
sections.content: Your pay stub contains important information. Here are the key sections:

interactive.title: Decode This Paycheque!
interactive.instruction: Click on each section of the pay stub to learn what it means

keyTakeaways: Gross income is what you earn; net income is what you take home
Typical deductions: federal tax, provincial tax, CPP, EI
Keep all your pay stubs - you'll need them for taxes!
Your deductions help fund important programs

content.introduction: Even if you only earned $5,000 from your part-time job, filing a tax return can put money back in your pocket and start building your financial history!

reasons.title: 💰 Get Money Back!
reasons.description: If you earned under $15,000, you likely paid too much tax. Filing gets you a refund!
reasons.example: Emma earned $7,000 at her summer job. $400 was deducted for taxes. She filed her return and got ALL $400 back!

reasons.title: 📈 Build RRSP Room
reasons.description: Every year you file creates contribution room for future retirement savings.
reasons.longTermBenefit: File now, even with zero income, and you'll have more room to save later

reasons.title: 🎓 Claim Education Credits
reasons.description: Tuition, textbooks, and student loan interest can be claimed.
reasons.savings: Post-secondary students can save $1,000+ per year

reasons.title: 💳 Build Credit History
reasons.description: Filing taxes helps establish your identity with financial institutions.
reasons.benefit: Makes it easier to get credit cards, loans, and apartments later

reasons.title: 📝 Required for Benefits
reasons.description: Many government benefits require you to file taxes annually.

sections.heading: What Happens If You Don't File?
consequences: ❌ Miss out on refunds (average teen refund: $300-500)
❌ May face penalties if you owe tax
❌ Harder to get student loans or financial aid

sections.heading: The Filing Process is Easy!

steps.timing: You'll receive these by end of February

sections.tip: First-time filers can't use NETFILE - you'll need to mail your first return. But after that, it's all online!

interactive.title: Calculate Your Potential Refund
interactive.description: Enter your part-time job income to see if you're owed money!
interactive.calculation: Basic refund estimate based on personal exemption

keyTakeaways: Filing taxes can get you hundreds of dollars back
Builds RRSP room for future savings
Required for many government benefits
Easy to do with free software
Start the habit early!

content.introduction: Your Social Insurance Number (SIN) is like your financial fingerprint. Protecting it is crucial!

sections.heading: What is a SIN?
sections.content: A Social Insurance Number is a 9-digit number issued by the Canadian government. You need it to work, pay taxes, and access government programs.
sections.importance: Your SIN is linked to all your earnings, taxes, and government benefits for life

sections.heading: When You SHOULD Give Your SIN
validUses: ✅ Starting a new job (employer needs it)
✅ Filing your tax return (CRA needs it)
✅ Opening an RRSP or TFSA (bank needs it)
✅ Applying for EI or other government benefits

sections.heading: When You SHOULD NOT Give Your SIN
invalidUses: ❌ Getting a credit card (they don't need it)
❌ Renting an apartment (landlord doesn't need it)
❌ Anyone asking via phone, email, or text
sections.warning: ⚠️ The CRA will NEVER call, text, or email asking for your SIN!

sections.heading: Protecting Your SIN
tips: 📝 Don't carry your SIN card in your wallet
🔒 Store it in a safe place at home
🚫 Never share it on social media
👀 Question anyone who asks for it
📱 Don't save it on your phone
💻 Don't enter it on unsecure websites

sections.heading: Signs of SIN Identity Theft
redFlags: CRA says you have income you didn't earn
You receive tax slips from companies you never worked for
Someone files a tax return in your name
You're denied government benefits you should qualify for
sections.action: If you suspect identity theft, call Service Canada immediately: 1-800-206-7218

scenarios.situation: A store cashier asks for your SIN to process a return
options: Refuse and ask why they need it
scenarios.explanation: Stores never need your SIN. Ask for a manager if they insist.

scenarios.situation: Your new employer asks for your SIN on your first day
scenarios.explanation: Employers legally need your SIN to report your earnings to CRA.

scenarios.situation: You receive a text claiming to be from CRA asking for your SIN
scenarios.explanation: CRA never contacts you via text. This is always a scam!

keyTakeaways: Your SIN is for work, taxes, and government programs only
Never give your SIN to stores or random requests
Store your SIN card safely at home, not in your wallet
CRA never calls, texts, or emails for your SIN
Report suspected identity theft immediately

content.introduction: Every February, you'll receive T4 slips from each employer you worked for in the previous year. Let's decode what all those boxes mean!

sections.heading: What is a T4 Slip?
sections.content: A T4 is an official document your employer must give you showing how much you earned and how much tax was deducted.
sections.deadline: Employers must provide T4s by February 28
sections.formats: You might receive it by mail, email, or through an online portal

boxes.name: Employment Income
boxes.whyItMatters: This is your gross income for the year

boxes.name: Employee's EI Premiums
boxes.whyItMatters: Insurance if you lose your job

boxes.name: Income Tax Deducted
boxes.description: Total federal + provincial tax taken off
boxes.whyItMatters: You might get some or all of this back!

mistakes.fix: If you had 3 jobs, wait for 3 T4s before filing
Double-check you're putting Box 14 in the right place
Contact your employer for a copy (they can reissue it)
Wait until late February or early March to file

interactive.title: Match the T4 Box to Its Meaning
interactive.instruction: Drag each box number to its correct description

keyTakeaways: T4 slips arrive by end of February
Box 14 shows your total income
Box 22 shows tax deducted (possible refund!)
You need ALL your T4s before filing
Keep T4s for at least 6 years

quiz.title: Tax Basics Final Assessment
quiz.description: Test your knowledge! Pass with 70% to earn your Tax Basics badge.

questions.question: Which of these services is primarily funded by taxes?
questions.explanation: Public hospitals are funded by taxes. Private services like Netflix, private schools, and restaurants are paid for directly by customers.

questions.question: What is the difference between gross and net income?
options: Gross is after deductions, net is before
Gross is before deductions, net is after
questions.explanation: Gross income is what you earn BEFORE deductions. Net income (take-home pay) is what you receive AFTER deductions.

questions.question: You should carry your Social Insurance Number card in your wallet for emergencies.
questions.explanation: FALSE! Never carry your SIN card in your wallet. Store it safely at home. If your wallet is stolen, your SIN could be used for identity theft.

questions.question: What does CPP stand for and what is it for?
options: Canadian Payment Plan - pays for healthcare
Canada Pension Plan - savings for retirement
Car Payment Program - helps buy vehicles
Credit Protection Plan - protects credit cards
questions.explanation: CPP is Canada Pension Plan. The money deducted from your paycheque goes into a pension that you'll receive when you retire.

questions.question: If you earned $7,000 in a part-time job and had $400 deducted for taxes, should you file a tax return?
options: Yes, you'll likely get a refund
Only if your parents tell you to
questions.explanation: YES! With $7,000 income, you're under the basic personal amount ($15,000+), so you likely paid too much tax. Filing will get you most or all of that $400 back!

questions.question: Which box on a T4 slip shows your total employment income?
questions.explanation: Box 14 shows your total employment income (gross pay) for the year. This is the amount you earned before any deductions.

questions.question: The CRA might call, text, or email you to ask for your Social Insurance Number.
questions.explanation: FALSE! The CRA will NEVER call, text, or email asking for your SIN. This is always a scam. Report it immediately.

questions.question: What is EI (Employment Insurance) used for?
options: Income if you lose your job
questions.explanation: EI provides temporary income if you lose your job through no fault of your own. It's insurance against unemployment.

questions.question: By when must employers provide T4 slips to employees?
questions.explanation: Employers must provide T4 slips by February 28 (or 29 in leap years) for the previous tax year.

questions.question: Which is a valid reason to give someone your Social Insurance Number?
options: A store asks for it to process a return
A new employer asks for it on your first day
Someone calls claiming to be from CRA
An online form requests it for a contest
questions.explanation: Employers legally need your SIN to report your earnings to the CRA. Never give your SIN to stores, callers, or random online forms.
